::: center
**Handout 29\
Comparing multiple means: ANOVA $F$ procedures**
:::

::: {#exer:knee .exer}
**Exercise 1**.

A recent double blind experiment[^1] investigated the effectiveness of
arthroscopic knee surgery relative to placebo surgery. Subjects were
randomly assigned to receive one of three treatments: arthroscopic
lavage (which involved flushing the knee joint with fluid), arthroscopic
debridement (which involved both lavage and shaving of cartilage and
removal of debris), and placebo surgery (which involved incisions in the
knee, but no insertion of instruments). Various outcomes were measured;
the JMP output below summarizes data on self-reported pain score two
years after the procedure on a knee-specific pain scale (0-100, with
with higher scores indicating more severe pain).
:::

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/knee_surgery_JMP_summary){width="70%"}

::: my_enumerate
State the null and alternative hypotheses (in words is fine).

Suggest a statistic which could be used to measure, in a single number,
how different the sample means are.
:::

::: my_itemize
Comparing multiple groups regarding a numerical response variable

The null hypothesis is (usually) that the true mean value of the
response variable is the same for each explanatory variable group
(population/process/treatment).

The alternative hypothesis is not $H_0$; that is, there is at least some
difference between the groups in terms of the means.

Side-by-side dotplots/histograms/boxplots, on the same axis scale, and
the group sample means and SDs summarize the observed data.

We want a statistic that measures in a single number how different the
observed data, i.e. the sample means, are from what we would expect when
the null hypothesis is true.

While there are several statistics that can be used, we will focus on
the most commonly used one, called the **$F\;$statistic** (named after
the statistician R.A. Fisher).\
:::

:::: exer

::::: my_enumerate
Rank the plots in order from weakest to strongest evidence to reject the
null hypothesis of no difference in means between treatments. That is,
rank the plots in order from largest to smallest p-value.
$$\begin{aligned}
& \text{weakest evidence to reject $H_0$} &\qquad \qquad \qquad  & \text{strongest evidence to reject $H_0$} \\
& \text{largest p-value} &\qquad \qquad \qquad  & \text{smallest p-value}
\end{aligned}$$

Compare plots A and B.

::: my_itemize
The variability *between* groups in Plot B is
$$\text{greater than} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{less than} \quad \qquad \qquad \text{the same as}$$
the variability *between* groups in Plot A.\

The variability *within* groups in Plot B is
$$\text{greater than} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{less than} \quad \qquad \qquad \text{the same as}$$
the variability *within* groups in Plot A.\
:::

Compare plots B and C.

::: my_itemize
The variability *between* groups in Plot C is
$$\text{greater than} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{less than} \quad \qquad \qquad \text{the same as}$$
the variability *between* groups in Plot B.\

The variability *within* groups in Plot C is
$$\text{greater than} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{less than} \quad \qquad \qquad \text{the same as}$$
the variability *within* groups in Plot B.\
:::

Rank the plots in order from smallest to largest $F$ statistic.
:::::

:::: my_itemize
The plots illustrate the idea behind the $F$ statistic: we reject the
null hypothesis of no difference in means between treatments
(populations) if the observed variability *between* groups is large
relative to the observed variability *within* groups.

That is, we reject the null hypothesis if the ratio
$$\frac{\text{variability between groups}}{\text{variability within groups}}$$
is large enough. This idea is known as **analysis of variance (ANOVA)**.

::: my_itemize
The name ANOVA refers to *what* we are doing, and not *why* we are doing
it.

Remember, we are analyzing the variance to make a conclusion about the
*means*
:::

The $F$ statistic quantifies the above ratio. The larger the value of
the $F$ statistic the stronger the evidence to reject the null
hypothesis (of no difference) in favor of the alternative hypothesis (of
some difference).\
::::

::: exer
**Exercise 3**. Continuing Exercise [1](#exer:knee){reference-type="ref"
reference="exer:knee"}. The computation of the $F$ statistic is full of
technical details. We will only do a rough hand computation which
illustrates the main ideas, relying on software to do the actual
computation for us. (If you're interested, the technical details are
included later in the handout.) The computation is somewhat simplified
when the sample size is the same for each explanatory variable group.
:::

::::::::::::::: my_enumerate
What statistic can be used to measure the variability *within* the
Debridement group? Lavage? Placebo? How could you combine these numbers
to to measure, in a single number, *variability within groups*?

::: my_itemize
The SD within each group measures the variability of the response
variable within that group.

The $F$ statistic works with *variances* to measure variability.

If the true variance within all groups is the same, we can pool the
observed sample variances from all the groups together to get a single
estimate of the true variance of the response.

To get an overall measure of the variability within groups, compute[^2]
the *mean of the group variances*, which becomes the denominator of the
$F$ statistic.\
:::

If the null hypothesis is true, what would you expect about the group
means? What statistic can be used to measure the variability *between*
groups?

::: my_itemize
If the null hypothesis is true, the group labels are meaningless, so
essentially we have one big sample instead of separate samples for each
group. (In this example, if the null hypothesis is true, we really just
have one big sample of 180, instead of 3 samples of 60 each.)

If the null hypothesis is true, we would expect the mean for each group
to be close to the overall mean.

We can measure how different the group means are from the overall mean
by computing the *variance of the group means*.\
:::

Regardless of whether or not the null hypothesis is true, which value
--- (a) or (b) --- would you expect to be larger? Why?

The variance of group means (in the numerator) plays the role of the
observed difference between groups. Even if the null hypothesis is true,
we would expect some variability between the group means just by chance;
how could we estimate this degree of variability?

:::: my_itemize
The means of the group variances (in the denominator) is roughly
$\sigma^2$, the population standard deviation of individual values of
the response (assuming the SD does not depend on group)

When the null hypothesis is true, we would expect some variability in
the group means just by chance. If the null hypothesis is true, the
variance of the group sample means (in the numerator) is roughly
$\sigma^2/n$, where $n$ is the common group size (e.g. $n=60$)

To effectively put the two variability measures --- between (variance of
means) versus within (variance of individual values) --- on a comparable
scale, multiply the numerator by the group size

::: my_itemize
The denominator --- based on the mean of group variances --- represents
the variability we would expect just due to chance when the null
hypothesis is true

The numerator --- based on the variance of group means --- represents
the degree of variability between groups we actually observe in the data

The larger the observed variability between groups is relative to what
is expected when the null hypothesis is true, the stronger the evidence
to reject the null hypothesis.
:::

The **one-way ANOVA $F$ statistic** when the group size $n$ is the same
for all $g$ groups is $$\begin{aligned}
F & = \frac{\text{group size} \times \text{variance of group means}}{\text{mean of group variances}}\\
%& = \frac{n\sum_{j=1}^g \left(\xbar_j-\bar{\xbar}\right)^2/(g-1)}{\sum_{j=1}^g s_j^2/g }
\end{aligned}$$
::::

Compute the $F$ statistic. What value would you expect $F$ to be if the
null hypothesis is true?

Specify in detail how the null distribution of the $F$ statistic could
be simulated with cards, and how you could use the results of the
simulation to compute the p-value.

The following plot displays results from an applet used to run 10000
repetitions of the simulation. Would a Normal distribution approximation
be appropriate? How could you use the applet to estimate the p-value?

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/knee_surgery_applet){width="20%"}

::: my_itemize
To hypothetically replicate the study assuming the null hypothesis is
true, we assume that the observed response of the units would be the
same regardless of what explanatory variable group they were in

The null distribution of the $F$ statistic has a mean of about 1.

The larger the value of the $F$ statistic the stronger the evidence to
reject the null hypothesis (of no difference) in favor of the
alternative hypothesis (of some difference).

So the p-value is the proportion of repetitions for which the simulated
$F$ statistic is at least as large as the observed $F$ statistic. That
is, the p-value in an $F$ test always corresponds to the right tail of
the null distribution.

The null distribution of the $F$ statistic will be skewed to the right,
even when the sample size is large.

If the null hypothesis is true the $F$ statistic has an **$F$
distribution with $g-1$ degrees of freedom in the numerator and $N-g$
degrees of freedom in the denominator**, denoted $F_{g-1,N-g}$,
approximately (given the assumptions of the method are satisfied; see
the box at the end of the handout for details)\
:::

State a conclusion in context. Are the results "significant"?

If we were to compute a series of pairwise confidence intervals for the
difference in group means --- Debridement $-$ Lavage, Debridement $-$
Placebo, Lavage $-$ Placebo --- what value would each of the confidence
intervals contain? Why?

::: my_itemize
The calculations relating to an $F$ statistic are traditionally
summarized in an **ANOVA table**\
\
![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/knee_surgery_anova_table){width="70%"}
:::

  Lavage            60   66.7   24.2
  Placebo           60   42.5   25.1

In comparison to the actual study data,

::: my_itemize
The $F$ statistic is
$$\text{farther from 0} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{closer to 0} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{exactly the same}$$

The p-value is
$$\text{farther from 0} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{closer to 0} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{exactly the same}$$

The evidence for rejecting the null hypothesis is
$$\text{stronger than} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{weaker than} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{exactly the same}$$
:::

In comparison to the actual study data,

The $F$ statistic is

The p-value is
$$\text{farther from 0} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{closer to 0} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{exactly the same}$$

::: exer
**Exercise 4**. When newborn babies eat, how long do they tend to eat
for? Does the length of time feeding vary with age? We'll investigate
using a small sample of two-week-old bottle-fed babies.
:::

::::: my_enumerate
Use R to conduct the ANOVA $F$ test.

The p-value is $<0.0001$. State the conclusion of the ANVA $F$ test in
context.

Consider the conclusion of the $F$ test. What are some natural follow-up
questions? How might you use the data to answer them?

:::: my_itemize
Rejecting the null hypothesis based on an $F$ statistic only tells you
that "the mean for at least one of the treatments (populations) is not
the same as the mean for at least one of the other treatments
(populations)".

The natural follow-up questions are: which treatment (population) means
differ? and by how much?

One approach when you have rejected the null hypothesis is to calculate
--- using software --- all pairwise confidence intervals. In particular,
which intervals do not contain zero?

When computing multiple confidence intervals, the multiple ($z^*$ or
$t^*$) should be increased[^3] to account for the **issue of multiple
comparisons**.

::: my_itemize
For example, with a multiple of 2 in a *single* confidence interval, we
are 95% confident that the interval contains the corresponding
parameter.

However, if we use a multiple of 2 for each of 10 confidence intervals,
we are only 60% confident[^4] that *all* of the 10 95% confidence
intervals contain their respective parameters.
:::

**Tukey's method** is a widely used method for constructing simultaneous
confidence intervals for *all pairwise comparisons of means*. The
confidence intervals computed using Tukey's method already contain an
adjustment to account for multiple comparisons.\
::::

Use R to create the Tukey confidence intervals. For which pairs would
you conclude the means are different? By how much?

Some of the babies in the data set were observed at multiple ages. Which
assumption of the ANOVA $F$ test does this violate?
:::::

**Hypothesis test for comparing multiple means: "One-way ANOVA $F$
test"**

::::::::::: my_itemize
Situation: numerical response variable; categorical explanatory variable

Parameters: $\mu_j$'s are the population/process/treatment response
means; $\sigma$ is the common group SD of responses

Goal: test for any differences in means

The null hypothesis is $H_0: \mu_1=\cdots=\mu_g$ ("no difference" or "no
treatment effect")

The alternative hypothesis is not $H_0$; that is, there is some
difference in means between groups,
$H_1: \mu_j\neq \mu_k \text{ for some } j\neq k$

Test statistic: one-way ANOVA $F$ statistic
$$F = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^g n_j\left(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x}\right)^2/(g-1)}{\sum_{j=1}^g (n_j-1)s^2_j/(N-g)}$$

The p-value is the probability of observing a value at least as large as
the observed $F$ based on an $F$ distribution with $g-1$ degrees of
freedom in the numerator and $N-g$ degrees of freedom in the
denominator, denoted $F_{g-1,N-g}$

Assumptions:

::::: my_itemize
Either

:::: my_itemize
The data are obtained through multiple unbiased and independent random
samples from large populations

::: my_itemize
Or from one unbiased random sample which can be classified into multiple
groups, and the groups can be considered independent of each other.
:::

The data are obtained from an experiment in which subjects were to two
treatments.
::::

No bias in data collection

Comparing *means* is an appropriate analysis

Equal variance: True SD of responses is same, $\sigma$, for each
population/process/treatment. Typically satisfied through random
assignment. Might not be satisfied if the data are sampled from
different populations/processes. One rule of thumb is that the largest
observed sample SD should be no more than twice the smallest.
:::::

The **one-way ANOVA $F$ statistic** when the group size $n$ is the same
for all $g$ groups is $$\begin{aligned}
F & = \frac{\text{group size} \times \text{variance of group means}}{\text{mean of group variances}}\\
& = \frac{n\sum_{j=1}^g \left(\bar{x}_j-\bar{\bar{x}}\right)^2/(g-1)}{\sum_{j=1}^g s_j^2/g }
\end{aligned}$$

When the sample sizes are not the same for each group, we modify the
calculation of the $F$ statistic to account for the differences in
sample sizes, basically by taking weighted averages. $$\begin{aligned}
g & = \text{number of groups}\\
n_j & = \text{sample size of group $j$}\\
N & = n_1+\cdots +n_g = \text{total sample size}\\
x_{ij} & = \text{observed response value for $i$th individual in group $j$}\\
\bar{x}_j & = \text{sample mean of group $j$}\\
\bar{\bar{x}} & = \frac{n_1\bar{x}_1 + \cdots+n_g\bar{x}_g}{N} = \text{overall mean of response}\\
s_j & =  \text{sample SD of group $j$}
\end{aligned}$$

Denominator of $F$, which corresponds to the variability within groups:
If we assume that the true variance, $\sigma^2$, is the same for each
group, a reasonable estimate of the variability *within* groups is the
pooled sample variance $$\begin{aligned}
s^2 & = \frac{1}{N-g}\sum_{j=1}^g\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} \left(x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j\right)^2 \\
& = \frac{1}{N-g}\sum_{j=1}^g (n_j-1)s^2_j
\end{aligned}$$

:::: my_itemize
The sum above is called the **error (or residual) sum of squares (SSE)**
or **SS(within)**

There are $N-g$ **degrees of freedom within groups**, or
$\textbf{df(within)}= N-g$.

Dividing SS/df yields $s^2$, which is also called the **mean square
error (MSE)** or **MS(within)**

::: my_itemize
When the group sizes are all the same:
$$s^2 = \frac{1}{g} \sum_{j=1}^g s_j^2\quad \text{ if } n_j=n, \; j=1,\ldots,g$$
:::
::::

Numerator of $F$, which corresponds to the variability between groups:
If the null hypothesis is true, then $\bar{\bar{x}}$ is a reasonable
estimate for the true common mean $\mu$. To measure the variability
*between* groups we measure how far each group sample mean varies from
the overall mean, scaled by the group sample sizes
$$\text{MS(between)} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^g n_j\left(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x}\right)^2}{g-1}$$

:::: my_itemize
The sum in the numerator above is called the **treatment (or model) sum
of squares (SSTr)** or **SS(between)**

There are $g-1$ **degrees of freedom between groups**, or "model degrees
of freedom", or $\textbf{df(between)}= g-1$.

Dividing SS/df yields the **mean square due to treatment (or model)
(MSTr)** or **MS(between)**

::: my_itemize
When the group sizes are all the same:
$$\text{MS(between)} = \frac{n\sum_{j=1}^g \left(\bar{x}_j-\bar{\bar{x}}\right)^2}{g-1}\quad \text{ if } n_j=n, \; j=1,\ldots,g$$
:::
::::

The **one-way ANOVA $F$ statistic** is $$\begin{aligned}
F & = \frac{\text{MS(between)}}{\text{MS(within)}}\\
& = \frac{\text{SS(between)}/\text{df(between)}}{\text{SS(within)}/\text{df(within)}}\\
& =\frac{\sum_{j=1}^g n_j\left(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x}\right)^2/(g-1)}{\sum_{j=1}^g (n_j-1)s^2_j/(N-g)}
\end{aligned}$$

If the null hypothesis is true the $F$ statistic has an **$F$
distribution with $g-1$ degrees of freedom in the numerator and $N-g$
degrees of freedom in the denominator**, denoted $F_{g-1,N-g}$
approximately.

The calculations are traditionally summarized in an **ANOVA table**

::: center
  ------------------------------------ ------- -------------------------- -------------------------
  Source                                    df        SS (Sum of squares)          MS (Mean Square)
  Between groups (a.k.a. "treament")     $g-1$                SS(between)   SS(between)/df(between)
  Within groups (a.k.a. "error")         $N-g$                 SS(within)     SS(within)/df(within)
  Total                                  $N-1$   SS(between) + SS(within) 
  ------------------------------------ ------- -------------------------- -------------------------
:::

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/knee_surgery_anova_table){width="70%"}
:::::::::::

[^1]: Source: <http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259>

[^2]: If the group sizes are not the same, you would compute a weighted
    average.

[^3]: There are several ways to do this. The simplest is a *Bonferroni*
    adjustment, which splits the error rate evenly across all intervals.
    For example, for simultaneous 95% confidence in 10 intervals (i.e. a
    total error rate of 0.05), use the $t^*$ factor for 99.5% confidence
    ($0.995 = 1-0.05/10$), $t^*= 2.8$, instead of 2 when computing the
    intervals. But the Tukey method is more widely used when comparing
    means.

[^4]: This number assumes independence of confidence intervals ---
    $0.95^{10}\approx 0.60$ --- but similar ideas apply more generally.
